SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, the hon. Minister, in his reply, 
has given details of the ten firms, which are well-known firms. But in view 
of the nature of stock operations, he would certainly appreciate that this, 
by itself, is not sufficient. My first question has two components. The first 
part of my question is: What is the long-term vision of this Government 
for a healthy growth of the stock market? The second part is: What is the 
total capital revenue earned by the stock market? What is the total revenue 
collection? This is important for capital gains—both long-term and short-
term. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, the long-term goal of the Government 
is to have a vibrant and well-regulated capital market, and I have dealt 
with this question at some length in my Budget speech where I have also 
suggested or proposed some measures that we are taking to make the 
capital market active, to broaden the market, to deepen the market and at 
the same time, to have a well-regulated market. I believe there can be no 
quarrel on this long-term goal. Every Government has set that, including 
the previous Government. That is a right goal to keep for ourselves as 
Government. If I understand the second part of the question: What is the 
extent of capital gains from the capital market? Frankly, it is very difficult 
to make an assessment. One can only make an inferential assessment, 
20 per cent of the trade and equity is delivered, 80 per cent is not delivered. 
We make that assessment, and we apply the average short-term capital 
gains rate which is between 10 and 35 per cent, and we also apply the 
long-term rate to a part of the transaction. There is an estimate which 
says that the Government may have collected about Rs. 2500 to 3500 
crores a year. There is no way whereby you can make an exact estimate 
because the capital gains is included in the individual return as part of his 
income-tax return, and as you know, 98 per cent of returns are free from 
scrutiny. In fact, last year, the Finan ce Minister freed, if I remember 
correctly, all the returns from scrutiny, to make the scrutiny process tax-
payer friendly. There is no way by which one can make an assessment. 
But inferentially, working back towards some figures, the Department 
estimates that in a normal year, it will gain between Rs. 2500 crores to 
Rs. 3500 crores by way of capital gains.

Modernisation of Madurai Airport 
*203. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to modernise and expand Madurai 
Airport and also to start aircraft operations from Salem Airport in Tamil 
Nadu; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Airports Authority of India (AAI) has phased plans for 
expansion and modernization of various infrastructure, facilities pertaining 
to air and city sides at Madurai Airport subject to handing over of the 
remaining required land measuring approximately six hectares by the State 
Government of Tamil Nadu to AAI. 
Salem Airport is an operational airport suitable for operation of B-737 
type of aircraft. No scheduled flight s are operating at present to/from 
Salem Airport. Airlines plan their operations based on commercial viability 
subject to route dispersal guidelines issued in this regard.

planned expansion and modernisation at the Madurai Airport. But as of 
now, approximately six hectares of land which is required by the Airports

(a) and (b) Pursuant to the announcement made by the Government

like plantation, horticulture, fisheries, organic farming, agro-
processing and other agricultural activities in the jurisdiction of

institutional credit;

of debt relief;

Governments at all levels is absolutely essential for the successful 
implementation of the package announced by the Government. Responses

*209. SHRIMATI SARLA MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state:

three years; 
(b) whether Government are having any short-term plan for the extension

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYA RANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
26

Statement 
As per provisional assessment made by the Ministry of Agriculture, 
the increase in area under irrigation during the last three years, i.e. during 
2001-02 to 2003-04 is of the order of 3.69 million hectare. 
Irrigation being a State subject, the responsibility of planning, execution 
and funding of all types of irrigation projects including drawing up of any 
short term plan for extension of irrigation facilities primarily rests with the 
State Governments. However, for early completion of ongoing major and 
medium irrigation projects, Government of India provides Central Loan 
Assistance (CLA) to the State Governments under the Accelerated 
Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97. CLA under AIBP is 
also provided for the minor Irrigation schemes of the special category 
States comprising the North Eastern States and Sikkim, the hilly States 
of J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttaranchal as well as the drought prone 
Kalahandi, Bolangir and Koraput districts of Orissa with effect from 1999-
2000. 
The Finance Minister in his budget speech for 2004-05 has given 
due thrust to AIBP. Further, he has also announced launching of schemes 
for repair, renovation and restoration of all water bodies that are directly 
linked to agriculture and water harvesting schemes.

Reduction in social sector spending by States 
*213. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are awar e that the cash strapped State 
Governments have been trying to bring their fiscal deficit under control 
by drastically cutting down their social sector spending; 
(b) whether Government are also aware that the reduced spending 
on social sector affects the vital public services leading to enhancement of 
poverty; 
(c) if so, whether Government have carried out any study to find out 
reasons for stagnation in the expenditure on social services by majority 
States; and 
34 

[20 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) the action Government propose to take in this matter? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) As per 
the latest report published by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in April, 
2004 on "State Finance—a Study of the Budgets 2003-04" the Gross 
Fiscal Deficit (GFD) of the State Governments as a proportion of Gross 
Domestic Product (GDP) declined from 4.7 per cent in 1999-2000 to 4.2 
per cent in 2001-02, but increased again to 4.7 per cent in 2002-03 (RE). 
It is budgeted at 4.2 per cent in 2003-04 (BE). The report further stated 
that although the aggregate social sector expenditure (comprising social 
services, rural development, food, storage and warehousing) of the States 
witnessed a rising trend in absolute terms over the last few years, as a 
percentage of total expenditure of States, it declined from 35 per cent in 
20U1 -02 to 33.5 per cent in 2002-03 (RE) and is budgeted at 33.5 per cent 
in 2003-04 (BE). As a percentage of GDP it increased from 5.8 per cent in 
2001-02 to 6 per cent in 2002-03 (RE) and is budgeted at 5.9 per cent in 
2003-04 (BE). 
(b) The Government are fully aware that development of the social 
sectors plays a vital role for eradication of poverty. The Central Government 
Budget for 2004-05 has announced various employment generation and 
poverty alleviation programmes. 
(c) The stagnation of expenditure on social services by majority of 
States is basically due to deteriorating State finances over the years. The 
proportion of States own revenue receipts to their total expenditure declined 
from 42.5 per cent in 2001-02 to 40.9 per cent in 2002-03 (RE) and is 
budgeted at 42.6 per cent in 2003-04 (BE) 
(d) Based on recommendations on the Eleventh Finance Commission, 
the Central Government has set up an Incentive Fund with a corpus of 
Rs. 10,607 crore earmarked over a period of five years for encouraging 
fiscal reforms in the States. The Central Government has drawn up a 
scheme called the "State Fiscal Reforms Facility" (2000-01 to 2004-05) 
under which the States draw up a Medium Term Fiscal Reform Plan 
(MTFRP) by setting monitorable target s on fiscal consolidation, public 
sector enterprises reform, power sector reforms and fiscal transparency. 
Incentive grants amounting to Rs. 3,278 crore have been released from 
the Incentive Fund to the States upto 30th September, 2003. The Planning 
Commission is also extending support to the MTFRP by ensuring that the 
annual plan framework is consistent with it.

drink plants;

40

DASMUNSI): (a) to (e) The Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) has 
examined utilisation of ground water by soft drink units located at 
Plachimada village, Palakkad district, Kerala and at Kaladera, Rajasthan.

0.02 m/yr to 0.9 m/yr and average 1.43 m/yr has been observed in an

concerned State Government to take remedial steps to check over-
exploitation of ground water. The following remedial measures are also 
envisaged in this regard by the Central Government: 
(i) Regulation of ground water withdrawal. 
(ii) Adopting artificial recharge. 
(iii) Treatment and recycling of industrial waste water. 
The CGWB has been asked to conduct special detailed studies to 
work out the actual volume of ground water used for the purposes of 
irrigation, domestic and industries with a view to know the factual position 
of use of ground water and its impact on ground water regime.

Disinvestment policy 
732. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated new disinvestment policy 
recently; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
64 

[20 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof and its basic difference from the one pursued 
by the previous Government; 
(c) the major public sector undertakings which were selected earlier 
for disinvestment but have since made a turn around; and 
(d) the estimated generation of resources as result of disinvestment in 
the next three years and how they are proposed to be spent? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Government is committed to a strong and effective public sector 
whose social objectives are met by its commercial functioning. But for 
this, there is need for selectivity and a strategic focus. It is pledged to 
devolve full managerial and commercial autonomy to successful, profit- 
making companies operating in a competitive environment. Generally profit 
making companies will not be privatised. 
All privatisations will be considered on a transparent and consultative 
case-by-case basis. The existing "Navaratna" companies will be retained 
in the public sector while these companies raise resources from the capital 
market. While every effort will be made to modernize and restructure sick 
public sector companies and revive sick industry, chronically loss-making 
companies will either be sold-off, or closed, after all workers have got their 
legitimate dues and compensation. The Government will induct private 
industry to turn around companies that have potential for revival. 
The Government believes that privatisation should increase competition, 
not decrease it. It will not support the emergence of any monopoly that 
only restricts competition. It also believes that there must be a direct link 
between privatisaiion and social needs —like, for example, the use of 
privatisation revenues for designated social sector schemes. Public sector 
companies and nationalised banks will be encouraged to enter the capital 
market to raise resources and offer new investment avenues to retail 
investors. 
The basic change that has been brought about through the above 
policy is that, under the new policy:- 
(a) the existing 'Navaratna' companies will be retained in the Public 
Sector, and (b) generally, profit-making companies will not be privatised. 
(c) Engineering Projects India Limited and Sponge Iron India Ltd. have 
since made a turn around from the time of the decision of the Government 
on the recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission.

P. Chidambaram, the hon. Financ e Minister, in this House on 8 th July. I am

policy-makers of this country have recognised the importance of agriculture on

Government doing for this sector? Just by saying that NABARD will be

that he is not playing a one-day match, and that he expects to

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI DINESH TRIVEDI) : Shri Lalit Suri. 
SHRI LALIT SURI (Uttar Pradesh): Si r, this is one of the rare 
occasions in the history when the basic fundamentals of Indian economy have 
been doing extremely well. In the year  2003-04, our GDP grew by 8.2 per 
cent. This is not that our agriculture only grew by nine per cent and our 
manufacturing sector grew by 6.7 per cent. Our foreign exchange reserves are 
on a record high. Food stocks are in abundance. Our economy had already 
fought and survived the cu rse of starvation, foreign exchange crisis and the 
era of double-digit inflation. 
Sir, the whole world recognises us as the fastest growing economies 
in the world. I am of the view that th is, therefore, was an occasion for radical 
steps to be taken in the Budget. It would have given a boost to the Indian 
economy. The Prime Minister has been  the Finance Minister during 1991-96. 
He was consistently a pro-reform person. The Finance Minister, Shri 
Chidambaram has also been identified with reforms. I would have, therefore, 
expected the combination of  the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister to 
take more progressive steps than they have taken in the Budget. 
Sir, I am conscious of the realities of politics and political 
compulsions, where some of the partners of the ruling Government, may have 
curbed the reform measures, which should have been taken, and have not 
been taken. In fact, some of the reform measures, which have taken place, 
are finding a lot of resistance. 
Our service sector has been doing well. Unfortunately, our agriculture 
still faces a challenge because of its dependence on monsoons. But the real 
area where the Finance Minister could have given more impetus is to the 
manufacturing sector. The manufacturing sector grew last year by 6.7 per 
cent. It is this sector, which gives a cutting edge to India over China. The 
manufacturing sector is where jobs are created; the manufacturing sector is 
where huge taxes are paid to the Government. Therefore, unless we are able 
to raise the growth rate of manufacturing 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [20 July, 2004]  
sector from 6.7 per cent to over 10 per  cent, the dream of 8 per cent growth 
rate will not become real. It is only a 8 per cent growth that can eradicate the 
curse of the poverty from the face of India. Gone are the days where the object 
of the economy was to distribute poverty. Today, the welfare of the country lies 
in the generation of wealth and its dist ribution to the people. Liberalisation 
since 1991 has proved that the fastest depletion of the number of people living 
below the poverty line has taken place in  the liberalisation era. How do we 
make the manufacturing sector grow? We need efficiencies; we need 
competitiveness. Let me underline some of the steps which are required to 
boost the manufacturing and service sector. 
We are heartened that the Finance Mini ster has recognized tourism, 
airports and seaports as focus areas of infrastructure with Rs. 40,000 crore 
pool for infrastructural growth. It has been recognized that India is going to 
become one of the major global tour ism destination country of the 21st century. 
International organizations have forecast  that tourism sector, which currently 
accounts for 17 million jobs in India, is  expected to sustain 25 million jobs by 
2011 which means over 1.10 million addi tional jobs annually over the next 
seven years. Domestic leisure touris m in India presents a huge prospective 
market of over 300 million people t hat is waiting to be tapped by making 
incremental investments in the necessary areas, which would go a long way to 
ensure improvement of the regions in which they are located. We are way 
behind in these areas and need a massive push and enablers such as better 
infrastructure, air-rail-road connecti vity, simplification of taxes and 
administrative procedures. Clearly, ther e are no major announcements in the 
Budget in this direction. 
From the corporate angle, the overall tax burden has been increased 
through the imposition of 2 per ce nt education cess and service tax 
enhancement. For the corporate sector, it is  not a 'cess' but a tax as the cess 
will be levied on top of the tax and the 10 per cent surcharge that they already 
pay. 
The 2 per cent cess on all taxes will amount to Rs. 5065.68 crore 
which is on tax receipts for 2003-04 of Rs. 2,53,285 crores. It means HRD 
ministry fund availability will go up to Rs. 9,797.76 crore as against Rs, 
4,732.08 crore allocated in the Budget. But the Ministry will have access to the 
cess money only after the Finance Bill is  passed and notified, possibly next 
month, to be spent in the remaining six months of the current financial year. It 
is also a matter of deep concern that hotels, which had 
164 

[20 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
been taken out of the ambit of service tax in the preceding two Budgets to 
dispel the perception of foreign visitors  and tourists of India as a high cost 
tourist destination country, have again been brought under the purview of 
service tax. The imposition of service ta x in this year's Budget on a larger 
number of services which include outdoor catering, pandal or shamiana 
service, airports services, etc., will adversely affect tourism and hospitality 
business. I urge the hon. Finance Minister to maintain status quo in respect of 
exemption of hotels from the purview of service tax as was done in the 
previous years. The proposed tax on aircraft leasing charges along with 
service charges on goods and other relate d activities at airport will create an 
extra burden of Rs. 600 crores to various domestic airlines. This will result in 
increase in fares, as the burden will be passed on to the customers. Small low 
cost airlines, with no frills, will be se verely affected. With the result, the 
customer will not get the ben efit of low cost travelling. This will severely harm 
both domestic and international tourists  and make our country a high-cost 
destination vis-a-vis our neighbouring countries. 
The Budget lacks in balancing the act of resource mobilization. 
Instead of adopting a proper route of ov erall fiscal reforms, it has gone along 
the lines of easy resources like cess and service tax. Firstly, we need world 
class infrastructure. We need highways, airports, sea ports, and transportation 
systems of global quality. The NDA Government had launched the National 
Highways Development Programme. It was a welcome initiative. I hope the 
UPA Government will expedite that with greater force. The Golden 
Quadrangle, the North-South, East-West Corridors, the Sager Mala are indeed 
great projects. The rural roads programme is a greater impetus to rural 
infrastructure. I am glad to  note that my friend, Mr. Praful Patel, is continuing 
the initiatives of the NDA Government towards the creation of world class 
airports in Delhi and Mumbai. Sea ports need investments. Airports are the 
gateway to India. Today, our airports are clumsy, inefficient and over-crowded. 
The Tourism Minister, Shrimati Renuka Chowdhury, has been espousing the 
dream of giving an impetus to touris m but she can forget improvement in 
tourism till such time that we are not able to at least double the number of 
seats in the flights to ensur e more tourists to India. For this to happen, we 
must have world class airports. Mumbai  Airport does not today have parking 
space for new aeroplanes. Airport ex tension needs investments. It needs 
professionalism. Airports are the gateways. Money will come from where 
money is available. I welcome the proposal  to raise the FDI in airports so that 
we are able to keep the best of foreign partners along with their Indian 
165 

RAJYA SABHA [20 July, 2004]  
counterparts to create the airports. But we should not limit ourselves to 
Mumbai and Delhi. It is of utmost  importance that upgradation and 
modernisation of these airports with state-of-the-art navi gational equipment 
shoutd be done. If there is any resistan ce, for whatever reasons, from Left 
parties or any other party, there should be an alternative plan to carry on with 
the modernisation of the airports by the Government so that the tourism is not 
affected. Kolkata can be the gateway of tra ffic from the east particularly to visit 
the Buddhist circuit. Bangalore, Ch ennai, Ahmedabad and Hyderabad are 
other important international airports we should be looking at. Our sea ports 
were nowhere amongst the efficient in the world. The entry of private parties in 
sea ports like Navasheva, Chennai and Tuticorin has brought new dimensions 
of efficiency into sea ports. This must continue. Efficiencies have made us 
more competitive. They have created more jobs. I welcome the proposal in the 
Budget to expedite the proposal to create a deep sea port at Valad Padam in 
Kochi. 
Secondly, to give a fillip to the manufacturing sector, we require to 
provide utilities, particularly power to our industries at international cost. I must 
caution against any move to review the Electricity Act, which has already been 
enacted. The principle on the basis of which public utilities survive is that users 
must pay. I can understand some subsidies being given to the farmers in 
matters of electricity tariff but we must check the theft and distribution losses, 
which are to the tune of 40 per cent. If power is stolen, given on concessional 
rates or even given free without metering, the entire burden of the power bill 
will fall on the industry. If our industry is given power on exorbitant prices, they 
cannot compete with the international competitors. 
Sir, thirdly, for any industry to survive, lending rate of interest must be 
internationally compatible. If the cost of interest on capital, which the Indian 
industry has to pay, is far in excess of their international competitors, then we 
should forget about thinking of making our industry internationally competitive. 
The interest rate regime, therefore, must continue to be liberalised. 
It is profitability that attracts invest ments, which, in turn, create jobs 
and employment. It brings more taxes, and revenue to the Government, which, 
in turn, boosts the economy. It is the em ployment and jobs that will help the 
economy grow and create wealth for the poor. 
166 

[20 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Lastly, trade facilitation is the ant ithesis of red tapism. Our ports, 
airports, customs, transportation system must be super efficient. International 
trade, which is curbed by red tapism, can add a huge amount to the cost. 
International studies have shown that a good facilitation can save up to 14 per 
cent of the costing. We must, ther efore, continue our endeavour towards 
efficiencies. 
We, today, live in a world where only the efficient is going to survive. 
The world, today, buys products and services from countries and sources 
where they consider it to be the cheapest and the best. We have done 
extremely well in the services sector, because our human capital being 
qualified and quality services as world class. We are doing extremely well in 
the manufacturing sector, particularly in automobiles, auto parts, textiles, 
pharmaceuticals, chemicals, because of our cost and quality. 
India has the best human capital to succeed, but the momentum of 
the Government policy and the Budget  should be to continue to make 
improvements, which I have suggested. My friends in the Left Parties must 
realise that even though they rightly have  a cause, in the rights of the working 
class, close to their hearts, the cause of  the working class will be served when 
jobs survive and new jobs are creat ed. Jobs will be created only in an 
environment of efficiencies and competitiv eness. Mere obstru ctionism to any 
form of reform will only promote inefficiency and non-competitiveness. 
Water is going to be one of the most crucial factors for the survival of 
human beings. I congratulate the Finance Minister for providing Rs. 1,000 
crore to put up a desalination plant in Chennai. I think this should be carried on 
to other cities, which are near sea. Wi th these words, I support the Budget and 
thank the Vice-Chairman for giving me this opportunity to express my views on 
the Budget.

opportunity. I have witnessed the most interesting discussion on the Union 
Budget. The Treasury Benches and the supporters of the UPA Government 
have naturally said that this is a Budget  that is relevant and have applauded it.

most significant comment that I pick ed up, particularly yesterday, was Mr. 
Jairam Ramesh' comment on the one hand, and Mr. Arun Shourie's on the 
other hand, that we need to evolve a medium- and long-term set of defined 
objectives and have the political will to implement those objectives in the 
interest of our country irrespective of which party we belong to. I am happy to 
observe from the comments that the emphasis on educ ation, health care and 
water is complemented by accelerated grass-root development. Having 
extensively toured my State of Karnataka,  it became very apparent to me that,

the rural level where it mattered most, I applaud the Finance Minister and his

to reduce fertilizer subsidies at the
